answers.primary: An MCP server: the vendor's remote HTTP MCP server added with `claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>` at user scope, with no credential passed on the command line, so each engineer completes the vendor's OAuth 2.0 browser flow themselves via `/mcp` (or `claude mcp login <name>`). The docs use exactly this shape for Sentry: it authenticates through OAuth rather than an API key, so you don't pass a credential when you add it. If the vendor ships an official plugin (for example `sentry` in the official marketplace), install that instead, since it is the same MCP server pre-configured.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill wrapping the vendor's REST API through Bash and curl. It would need a long-lived API key on disk or in an env var, which is precisely the credential model being rejected, and it gives no per-engineer identity or token refresh.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code owns the transport, the OAuth handshake, the stored token, and the refresh-and-retry on 401; it also owns which tools are exposed to the model. The model only decides to call the resulting tools.
answers.context_boundary: The MCP tool definitions and every tool result land in the main session context window and are billed there each turn. The OAuth handshake happens out of context in the engineer's browser, and the access token is held by Claude Code, so no credential ever enters the transcript.
answers.lifecycle: The server connects when the session starts and reconnects automatically; the OAuth flow is triggered on first use or whenever the server answers 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden, and can be run ahead of time with `claude mcp login`. An already-signed-in server that returns 401 gets its stored token refreshed and the request retried once. It stops applying when the server is removed, disabled, or the stored authorization is revoked.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed: an unauthenticated or unreachable server is flagged in `/mcp` and its tools simply are not offered, so engineers fall back to pasting stack traces by hand, which is the original problem returning silently. Two specific traps: if a static `headers.Authorization` is configured and the server rejects it, Claude Code reports the connection as failed instead of falling back to OAuth; and some Anthropic-hosted connectors cannot do local OAuth from Claude Code because the upstream identity provider only accepts the redirect URL claude.ai registered.
answers.version_caveat: OAuth authentication works with HTTP servers only, not the `ws` transport, which is header-only. `claude mcp login <name>` requires Claude Code v2.1.186 or later. Before v2.1.206, a token refresh that failed for a transient reason such as a network error flagged the server as needing authentication for the rest of the session even though the refresh token was still valid. `--callback-port` is available when the vendor requires a pre-registered redirect URI.

answers.primary: An LSP server delivered as a plugin: install `typescript-lsp` from the official `claude-plugins-official` marketplace, after installing the `typescript-language-server` binary. That plugin is just a `.lsp.json` mapping `.ts`/`.tsx` to the language server, and it turns on both halves of the request: automatic diagnostics pushed into Claude's context after every edit, and code navigation (go to definition, find references, hover, implementations, call hierarchies) instead of grep.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PostToolUse hook running `tsc --noEmit` after each Write or Edit. It catches type errors but is a full project typecheck per edit rather than incremental server diagnostics, and it gives no definitions, references, or hover, so it solves only half the need at much higher latency.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code starts and supervises the language server process, and pushes diagnostics into Claude's context after edits on its own (`diagnostics` defaults to true). The model does not choose to run the typechecker.
answers.context_boundary: The language server runs out of context as a subprocess owned by Claude Code. Only the diagnostic summaries after each edit and the results of explicit navigation requests cross into the main session context; the server's full index and protocol traffic never do. The user sees an indicator such as 'Found 3 new diagnostic issues in 2 files' and presses Ctrl+O to read them.
answers.lifecycle: The server starts when the plugin is enabled and the session begins, claims the file extensions declared in `extensionToLanguage`, and runs for the session. `/reload-plugins` restarts plugin LSP servers. It stops applying when the plugin is disabled, when the server crashes past `maxRestarts`, or when another enabled server registered the same extension first, in which case this one never starts at all.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open, which is the dangerous shape here: if the binary is missing you get `Executable not found in $PATH` in the `/plugin` Errors tab and Claude quietly goes back to grepping, with no error at the point of use. A configuration that is invalid (missing `command` or `extensionToLanguage`) is skipped entirely, with the reason visible only under `claude --debug`. Other practical failures: large monorepos produce false-positive unresolved-import diagnostics, and servers like pyright and rust-analyzer can consume significant memory.
answers.version_caveat: `restartOnCrash` and `shutdownTimeout` require Claude Code v2.1.205 or later; before v2.1.205 the schema accepted both but setting either caused Claude Code to skip that LSP server entirely at startup, visible only in `claude --debug`. Also before v2.1.205, a server that failed to initialize still claimed its extensions and blocked another valid server for the same extension. The plugin never installs the language server binary for you.

answers.primary: A plugin distributed through a team marketplace, wired into each repository by settings rather than by copying files. Put the review helpers in `skills/`, the workflow commands in `skills/` or `commands/`, the edit-time automations in `hooks/hooks.json`, and the external-tool configuration in the plugin's own `.mcp.json`, publish it from a git-hosted marketplace, then add `extraKnownMarketplaces` plus `enabledPlugins` to each repository's `.claude/settings.json`. When team members trust the repository folder, Claude Code prompts them to install these marketplaces and plugins.
answers.rejected_alternative: Committing a `.claude/` directory with standalone skills, commands and hooks into every repository. It gives no versioning and no update path: each of the many repositories holds its own drifting copy that someone has to re-sync by hand every time the platform team publishes a change.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness for loading and updating (Claude Code reads `extraKnownMarketplaces`/`enabledPlugins`, resolves the marketplace, installs and auto-updates), with a human consent gate: the engineer must trust the workspace folder and accept the install prompt. The model owns nothing here.
answers.context_boundary: Plugin components load into each engineer's main session context: skills and agents as loadable definitions, MCP tool schemas as tool definitions, with a per-turn token cost the `/plugin` detail view estimates as 'Context cost'. Hooks and MCP servers execute in their own processes outside the context window and only their output crosses back.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered when an engineer opens a repository whose `.claude/settings.json` names the marketplace and trusts the folder; Claude Code then prompts to install. Updates arrive through marketplace auto-update, which runs in the background after session start with a random delay of up to ten minutes, so the running session keeps its loaded versions until `/reload-plugins` or the next launch. It stops applying when the plugin is disabled or uninstalled, or when the marketplace is removed, which uninstalls everything installed from it.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open at the consent boundary: the set is offered, not imposed. An engineer who declines the trust prompt or the install prompt simply works without the helpers and hooks, silently, so you get inconsistent enforcement across the team rather than a hard failure. Auto-update is disabled by default for third-party marketplaces, so without turning it on people sit on stale versions. To actually mandate the set you need managed settings, which install at managed scope and cannot be modified by users.
answers.version_caveat: As of Claude Code v2.1.195 the install step applies on every path that loads plugins: a plugin that only the project's `.claude/settings.json` enables, and that comes from an external source such as a GitHub repository or npm package, does not load until the team member installs it, and Claude Code reports it as not installed. The scope-choice dialog when uninstalling a project-enabled plugin requires v2.1.203 or later. Administrators can set `"autoUpdate": true` on each `extraKnownMarketplaces` entry in managed settings.

answers.primary: A plugin with a `bin/` directory holding the deployment binary (or a thin wrapper that execs it). Files in a plugin's `bin/` are added to the Bash tool's `PATH` and are invokable as bare commands in any Bash tool call while the plugin is enabled, so Claude can write `deploy status | jq '.services[]' | grep degraded` with no absolute path and nobody edits their shell profile.
answers.rejected_alternative: Wrapping the CLI in an MCP server so each subcommand becomes a tool. That loses exactly what was asked for: MCP tool results come back as tool output, not as a stream you can pipe into `grep` and `jq`, and every subcommand would have to be modelled as a separate tool schema that costs context on every turn.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code injects the plugin's `bin/` onto the `PATH` of the Bash tool's environment while the plugin is enabled. The model just types the bare command name; it is not responsible for locating the binary.
answers.context_boundary: The binary executes in a Bash subprocess, entirely outside the context window. Only the pipeline's stdout and stderr cross back into the main session context, so a large subcommand dump is a context cost the model must manage with `head`, `jq` filters, or redirection. The binary's own help text and subcommand surface are not preloaded, which is why a skill documenting the subcommands is a useful companion.
answers.lifecycle: `PATH` injection is active for the whole time the plugin is enabled, from plugin load onward, and applies to every Bash tool call in every project the plugin is enabled for. It stops the moment the plugin is disabled or uninstalled. On a plugin update `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` changes, so anything resolving the binary by absolute path breaks while the bare name keeps working.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed at the shell: if the plugin is disabled, the file lacks the executable bit, or the shipped binary is the wrong OS/architecture for that engineer's machine, the command dies with 'command not found' or an exec error, and the model is prone to improvise a wrong absolute path or a substitute command instead of reporting the real cause. The injection is scoped to the Bash tool, so it does not help hook commands, monitors, or the engineer's own terminal, which is a common source of 'it works for Claude but not for me'.
answers.version_caveat: The plugin docs document `bin/` only as a default plugin-root folder, with no corresponding manifest key and no stated minimum Claude Code version or experimental gate, so unlike `monitors` and `themes` it is not an experimental component. The practical gate is not a version but packaging: shipping a compiled binary through a marketplace means shipping per-platform builds, since the plugin is copied verbatim into `~/.claude/plugins/cache` and cannot reference files outside its own directory.

answers.primary: A plugin published from a git-hosted marketplace with commit-SHA versioning: omit the `version` field from both `plugin.json` and the marketplace entry, so Claude Code falls back to the git commit SHA of the plugin's source and users get updates on every new commit to the plugin's git source. Pair that with auto-update enabled on the marketplace so the refresh happens without anyone running `/plugin update`. The docs name this exact approach as the one for internal or team plugins under active development.
answers.rejected_alternative: Explicit semver in `plugin.json`. It is the wrong shape for a daily-changing bundle: users get updates only when you bump the field, so every merge would need a version bump, which is precisely the release bookkeeping being eliminated.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code computes the plugin's version, uses it as the cache key that decides whether an update is available, and runs the background auto-update. Neither the model nor the publisher touches the update path once the source is configured.
answers.context_boundary: Nothing about versioning enters the session context window. The update runs as background work on the user's machine; the newly loaded components announce themselves in content appended to the conversation only after `/reload-plugins` or at the next launch.
answers.lifecycle: Auto-update fires after the session starts, with a random delay of up to ten minutes, so the running session keeps using the versions it loaded at launch. If plugins were updated you get a notification prompting `/reload-plugins`, otherwise the new versions load on the next launch. It stops when the plugin is uninstalled, when the marketplace is removed (which uninstalls its plugins), or when `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` is set.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and silently, in one specific way: if anyone sets `version` in `plugin.json` or in the marketplace entry, SHA-based versioning is bypassed and pushing new commits alone stops delivering anything, while `/plugin update` cheerfully reports 'already at the latest version'. The second silent failure is that auto-update is disabled by default for third-party and local development marketplaces, so without toggling it on, teammates keep whatever they installed. Also note that every merged commit reaching everyone means a bad commit reaches everyone too, with no release gate.
answers.version_caveat: Commit-SHA versioning only applies to `github`, `url`, `git-subdir`, and relative-path sources in a git-hosted marketplace; `npm` sources and local directories not inside a git repository resolve to the version `unknown` instead. Auto-update defaults to on only for official Anthropic marketplaces; administrators can set `"autoUpdate": true` on each `extraKnownMarketplaces` entry in managed settings. `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` turns off all automatic updates, and `FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS=1` keeps plugin updates while disabling Claude Code's own.

answers.primary: An MCP server entry using `headersHelper`: an `http` server pointing at the internal service, with `headersHelper` set to the SSO helper command, which Claude Code runs and whose JSON output it merges into the connection headers. The docs name this case directly as the mechanism for an authentication scheme other than OAuth, such as Kerberos, short-lived tokens, or an internal SSO. The helper must write a JSON object of string key-value pairs to stdout, for example `{"Authorization": "Bearer ..."}`.
answers.rejected_alternative: A static `headers` entry with `${TOKEN}` environment-variable expansion in `.mcp.json`. Environment expansion is resolved once at config load, so it cannot produce a fresh token when the old one expires mid-session, which is the whole requirement.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code executes the helper command, merges its output into the connection headers, and re-runs it on authentication failure. The model never sees or handles the token.
answers.context_boundary: The helper runs as a shell subprocess with a 10-second timeout, from the session's working directory, entirely outside the context window; only MCP tool results cross into the main session context. The minted token stays in the connection headers and never enters the transcript. Claude Code sets `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_NAME`, `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_URL`, and (for plugin-provided servers) `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` in the helper's environment so one script can serve several servers.
answers.lifecycle: The helper runs fresh on each connection, at session start and on every reconnect, with no caching, so your script is responsible for any token reuse. It also re-runs on demand: a tool call that returns 401 or 403 causes Claude Code to re-run the helper, reconnect with the fresh headers, and retry the call once. It stops applying when the server is removed or disabled.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed per call, with a narrow recovery window. Mid-session expiry is only covered by that single automatic retry; if the re-minted token is also rejected, Claude Code marks the server as needing authentication in `/mcp` and the tools go away for the rest of the session. The 10-second shell timeout is a real hazard when the SSO helper itself needs an interactive prompt or a slow network round trip, and because there is no caching a chatty session re-runs the helper on every reconnect. Dynamic headers silently override any static `headers` of the same name.
answers.version_caveat: The automatic re-run of the helper plus retry on 401/403 requires Claude Code v2.1.193 or later. For a plugin-provided server, resolving a relative `headersHelper` path against the plugin root requires v2.1.195 or later, and before v2.1.195 plugin `headersHelper` passed the `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` placeholder through as a literal string. A plugin-provided `headersHelper` cannot reference `${user_config.*}` values because the command is shell-parsed; before v2.1.207 it did substitute them. `headersHelper` executes arbitrary shell commands, so at project or local scope it only runs after the workspace trust dialog is accepted.

answers.primary: A plugin background monitor: add `monitors/monitors.json` at the plugin root with an entry whose `command` is `tail -F ./logs/error.log`, a `name`, a `description`, and `when` left at its default `"always"`. Claude Code starts each monitor automatically when the plugin is active, and every stdout line from the command is delivered to Claude as a notification during the session, which is precisely 'without anyone asking it to start watching'. This is the docs' own worked example.
answers.rejected_alternative: A SessionStart hook that launches `tail -F` as a background Bash process. The hook can start the process, but hook output is injected once at the hook's moment; it has no channel for pushing each subsequent line into the conversation as it appears, so it gives startup automation without the ongoing delivery.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code spawns the monitor process when the plugin is active and delivers each stdout line as a notification; the model does not decide to start or poll it, it only reacts to what arrives.
answers.context_boundary: The `tail` process runs as a persistent background process in the session working directory, outside the context window. Each stdout line crosses the boundary into the main session context as a notification, and the `description` is what shows in the task panel and notification summaries. Because every line crosses, the log's volume is directly a context cost.
answers.lifecycle: With `when` at `"always"` the monitor starts at session start and on plugin reload; `"on-skill-invoke:<skill-name>"` would instead start it the first time that skill is dispatched. It runs for the lifetime of the session. Notably, if you disable the plugin mid-session Claude Code does not stop monitors that are already running; they stop when the session ends. After a plugin update, monitors keep using the previous version's path and require a session restart rather than `/reload-plugins`.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and is silently skipped where unsupported, then floods where supported. Monitors run only in interactive CLI sessions, run unsandboxed at the same trust level as hooks, and are skipped on hosts where the Monitor tool is unavailable, so a CI or headless run just never watches anything and nobody is told. Where it does run, a noisy error log pushes an unbounded stream of notifications into the context window and can crowd out the actual task. The `name` field is what prevents duplicate processes when the plugin reloads, so a careless rename spawns a second tail.
answers.version_caveat: Monitors are an experimental plugin component: the manifest schema may change between releases, and declaring them at the top level of `plugin.json` still works but `claude plugin validate` warns and a future release will require `experimental.monitors`. Monitor commands cannot reference `${user_config.*}` values and are rejected with an error if they do; before v2.1.207 those values were substituted. The underlying Monitor tool is not available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry, nor when `DISABLE_TELEMETRY` or `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` is set.

answers.primary: An MCP server entry with `oauth.scopes` pinned to the read-only subset, for example `"oauth": { "scopes": "issues:read search:read" }` on the `http` server. The docs call this the supported way to restrict an MCP server to a security-team-approved subset when the upstream authorization server advertises more scopes than you want to grant. Because it pins the scopes requested during the authorization flow, the access token the vendor mints physically lacks write and admin, which is the credential-level guarantee asked for. Push it through managed settings so engineers cannot widen it locally.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook or a `deny` permission rule blocking the write-shaped MCP tools. That constrains what the assistant is allowed to call, not what the credential can authorize; the token on disk would still carry write scope and any other process, or a bypassed permission mode, could use it. The requirement explicitly rules out 'the assistant declines'.
answers.enforcement_owner: Ultimately the vendor's authorization server, with the harness owning the request. Claude Code sends the pinned `scope` parameter in the authorization request and stores whatever token comes back; the vendor decides what that token may do. The model is out of the loop entirely, which is the point.
answers.context_boundary: The authorization handshake happens out of context in the browser and the resulting token lives in Claude Code's credential storage, never in the transcript. Only the read-only tool definitions and their results cross into the main session context window.
answers.lifecycle: The pinned scopes apply at every authorization flow for that server, from the first sign-in onward, and `oauth.scopes` takes precedence over both `authServerMetadataUrl` and the scopes discovered at `/.well-known`. If the server later returns 403 `insufficient_scope` for a tool call, Claude Code re-authenticates with the same pinned scopes rather than escalating. It stops applying if the field is removed, at which point the MCP server determines the requested scope set again.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed against the credential, which is the desired behaviour: a write tool call comes back 403 `insufficient_scope` and re-authentication does not widen the grant. The residual risk is not technical but configurational: `oauth.scopes` is a config field, so at user or project scope an engineer can edit it and re-authenticate with broader scopes, and the guarantee only holds if it is deployed through managed settings. Note also that Claude Code appends `offline_access` to the pinned scopes when the authorization server advertises it in `scopes_supported`, so the effective grant is not byte-identical to what you wrote.
answers.version_caveat: The default behaviour when `oauth.scopes` is unset changed in v2.1.196: Claude Code now requests the scope from the server's `WWW-Authenticate` header or its protected resource metadata and sends no `scope` parameter when neither provides one, rather than requesting the full `scopes_supported` catalog. On earlier versions, leaving scopes unpinned against a provider that advertises admin scopes could request that whole catalog and be rejected with `invalid_scope`. Metadata fetched from a configured `authServerMetadataUrl` still supplies its `scopes_supported` as the requested scopes.

answers.primary: A project-scoped MCP server: add it with `claude mcp add --transport http staging-db --scope project <url>`, which writes `.mcp.json` at the project root, and check that file into version control so everyone on the team gets the same MCP tools and services. Project scope is the only one of the three that is shared via version control and is limited to the current project, which matches 'from a fresh clone' and 'no other repository' exactly.
answers.rejected_alternative: User scope (`--scope user`, stored in `~/.claude.json`). It is private to each machine so it would not arrive with a clone, and it is available across all your projects, which directly violates the 'no other repository will ever use this connection' constraint.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness, gated on a per-user consent prompt. Claude Code discovers `.mcp.json` in the project root, holds the server until the user approves it, and then owns the connection. The model has no say in whether the server loads.
answers.context_boundary: Config crosses into the repository through git; the server's tool definitions and results cross into each engineer's main session context window once approved. Credentials do not travel in `.mcp.json` if you use OAuth or `headersHelper`, which is why you should not embed a token there even though the file is shared.
answers.lifecycle: The server is discovered when a session opens in that project directory and connects once the user approves it; the approval is recorded per user so the prompt appears only on first use. `claude mcp reset-project-choices` clears those recorded approvals so the prompt returns. Scope precedence is local, then project, then user, so a same-named local entry silently wins over the shared one, with the entire entry taken from the winning source and no field merging.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed, which is safe but surprising in automation: for security reasons Claude Code prompts for approval before using project-scoped servers from `.mcp.json`, and until someone approves, `claude mcp list` and `claude mcp get <name>` show the server as 'Pending approval (run `claude` to approve)' with none of its tools present. A rejected server shows as 'Rejected (see disabledMcpjsonServers in settings)'. A non-interactive or CI session cannot answer the prompt, so it needs `enabledMcpjsonServers` in settings instead. The quiet failure is a teammate who declined once and then reports the tools 'missing' rather than 'not approved'.
answers.version_caveat: The scope names were renamed: older versions called today's `local` scope `project`, and today's `user` scope `global`, so older team documentation and scripts using `--scope project` may mean the private per-machine scope. Environment-variable expansion inside a project-scoped `.mcp.json` needs a default for session variables, for example `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}`, because that variable is set in the server's environment rather than Claude Code's own; plugin-provided configs substitute it directly and need no default.

answers.primary: A plugin `SessionStart` hook that installs into `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}`, the persistent directory that survives plugin updates and is documented for exactly this use: installed dependencies such as `node_modules` or Python virtual environments, generated code, and caches. Use the docs' recommended pattern rather than a bare existence check: `diff -q "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/package.json" "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/package.json" || (cd "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}" && cp "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/package.json" . && npm install) || rm -f "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/package.json"`, then point consumers at it with `NODE_PATH=${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/node_modules`.
answers.rejected_alternative: Running `npm install` into `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` from the same hook. That is the trap this scenario describes: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` changes when the plugin updates, so every update strands the installed modules in the old version directory, which is itself cleaned up automatically about two weeks later.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness runs the hook and resolves `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` (to `~/.claude/plugins/data/{id}/`, created on first reference), and the hook script owns the install decision. The model is not involved and is not asked to run `npm install`.
answers.context_boundary: The hook executes as a subprocess at session start, outside the context window; only whatever it writes to stdout crosses into the session context, so the install should stay quiet. The installed `node_modules` are then read by MCP or LSP subprocesses through `NODE_PATH`, also outside the context window. `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}`, and `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` are all exported as environment variables to hook processes and to MCP and LSP server subprocesses.
answers.lifecycle: Runs on `SessionStart`, every session, but does real work only on first run and after an update whose `package.json` differs from the stored copy, because `diff` exits nonzero when the stored copy is missing or differs. The data directory outlives any single plugin version and is deleted automatically when you uninstall the plugin from the last scope where it is installed.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open at install time and then breaks downstream: the session continues even if `npm install` fails, and the component that needed the modules errors later at first use, far from the cause. The pattern's trailing `rm` removes the copied manifest so the next session retries, which is a deliberate self-heal rather than a silent poison. The specific mistake the docs warn about is checking only for the directory's existence: because the data directory outlives any single plugin version, an existence check cannot detect when an update changes the plugin's dependency manifest, so users keep running against stale dependencies.
answers.version_caveat: Persistence is not unconditional: the data directory is deleted automatically on uninstall from the last scope, the `/plugin` interface shows its size and prompts first, and the CLI deletes by default unless you pass `--keep-data`. Related timing gates: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` changes on update and the previous version's directory is removed about 14 days later, and when a plugin updates mid-session hooks, MCP servers and LSP servers keep the old path until `/reload-plugins`, while monitors require a full session restart.
